item.title: Two decades of mass protests in India
item.description:
Thousands of supporters of India’s youth-led “cockroach” movement have been protesting since June, demanding the education minister resign over exam paper leaks, in the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his third term.

Activists say the leaks showed widespread corruption, a complaint which has brought crowds onto the streets for years. Following are details of major rallies, triggered by graft and other crimes and causes, over the past two decades.

April 2011

Anti-corruption activist Anna Hazare started the first of two hunger strikes in a bid to push the government to bring in anti-graft legislation.

Hundreds of thousands rallied to his support across the country and he was briefly jailed by the then-Congress alliance government.

India’s parliament eventually passed an anti-graft law, though Hazare said it watered down his demands. Some of his supporters went on to form the Aam Aadmi Party in 2012, now one of Modi’s opponents in parliament.

December 2012

Public fury over the gang-rape of a young woman on a moving bus in New Delhi erupted into mass protests in the capital.

Crowds blockaded roads, broke through police lines in street confrontations and called for an overhaul of a system and a society they said had failed to tackle violence against women. Many demanded the culprits be executed.

The 23-year-old woman died in a Singapore hospital a few days after the attack. In response, India amended laws to expand the definition of sexual assault and set up fast-track courts to speed up trials in such cases.

December 2019

India’s parliament passed a new citizenship law that brought hundreds of thousands of people to the streets in protests and triggered bouts of sectarian violence that killed at least 76 people.

The Citizenship Amendment Act aimed to fast-track citizenship for Hindus, Parsis, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains and Christians who arrived in India on or before December 31, 2014 from neighbouring Muslim-majority Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

Critics said the law, alongside a proposed national register of citizens, discriminated against Muslims and violated the spirit of India’s secular constitution. Some feared the government would remove the citizenship of Muslims without documents in some border states.

India implemented the law in March 2024.

September 2020

Thousands of farmers blocked roads and railway tracks in protests against new legislation that they say could pave the way for the government to stop buying grain at guaranteed prices, leaving them at the mercy of private buyers.

Modi’s government defended the bills, saying they would help rid India’s vast agriculture sector of antiquated laws and allow farmers to sell to institutional buyers and big retailers.

The protests lasted more than a year before Modi repealed the laws.

June 2022

An overhaul of military recruitment, designed to bring in fitter, younger troops and reduce pension expenditure, triggered rail blockades and protests across the country.

Recruits, veterans and opposition leaders objected to the introduction of fixed four-year contracts, saying people would struggle to get other jobs once their service was over.

Modi’s government refused to roll back the programme but offered instead to reserve 10 per cent of state vacancies for those who had served the four years.

August 2024

Thousands of doctors took to the streets for months after the rape and murder of a trainee doctor in a government hospital in the eastern city of Kolkata.

Protesters demanded safer workplaces, a crackdown on violence against women and a swift investigation into the attack.

item.title: The Karim Khan saga: a timeline
item.description:
The Karim Khan saga: a timeline

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Thu, 07/23/2026 - 14:09
How allegations against the ICC’s chief prosecutor became entangled with pressure over his pursuit of Israeli officials, culminating in a vote that could reshape the court
Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on 14 March 2025 (AFP/file photo)
Off

Member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) are due to vote at the United Nations' headquarters in New York on Friday on whether to remove the court's chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, from office – a first in the court’s 24-year history. 

The vote caps a saga stretching back more than two years, spanning sexual misconduct allegations Khan has consistently denied, a UN-led investigation, a judicial panel that unanimously cleared him, and a bureau that chose to override that finding and press ahead regardless.

The case has unfolded alongside a separate campaign of pressure on Khan and the court over his pursuit of war crimes warrants against Israeli and Hamas leaders, from a threat by Britain's then foreign secretary to defund the ICC, to sanctions imposed on Khan and dozens of ICC officials by the Trump administration, to the US secretary of state's public vow to "dismantle" the court.

Khan, a British barrister, is the ICC's third chief prosecutor since the court’s founding in 2002. 

In addition to seeking warrants for Israeli leaders, his office has sought arrest warrants for Russia’s Vladimir Putin, the Philippines' Rodrigo Duterte, Myanmar’s junta leaders, and Taliban officials in Afghanistan. 

Middle East Eye has been at the forefront of exclusive coverage of the misconduct case at all stages.

Below is a timeline of how the case unfolded, from early 2024 till the highly controversial 24 July vote.

Palestine investigation, and the pressure campaign begins (2021–2023)

February 2021 Karim Khan is elected ICC chief prosecutor by the Assembly of States Parties (ASP). 

March 2021 Khan's predecessor, Fatou Bensouda, opens the ICC's investigation into alleged war crimes in the occupied Palestinian territories.

21 June 2021 Khan takes the oath of office, becoming the third person to hold the post since the court's founding in 2002.

Summer 2022 The woman who later becomes the complainant in the sexual misconduct case alleges a separate senior ICC official behaved inappropriately towards her.

31 August 2022 Khan writes to the ASP president raising her concerns about that other official; external investigators are appointed in October 2022 with her cooperation.

11 December 2023 That separate external investigation concludes there was "no unsatisfactory conduct" by the official concerned.

17 November 2023 Five states (South Africa, Bangladesh, Bolivia, Comoros, Djibouti) formally refer the Palestine situation to the prosecutor after the 7 October Hamas attack on Israel and the subsequent Israeli war on Gaza.

December 2023 Khan visits Israel (kibbutzim, the Nova festival site) and meets Palestinian officials including President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah. 

Lead-up to the warrants (January–April 2024)

January 2024 Khan convenes an independent, seven-member expert panel to assess whether the legal threshold for arrest warrants for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his then Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, and three Hamas leaders had been met. The panel unanimously concludes in March the process was "fair, rigorous and independent" and sufficient material existed to request warrants.

16 March 2024 Khan's legal team concludes it will be in a position to apply for the Israeli and Hamas warrants by the end of April.

21 March 2024 Khan orders a "complementarity" check into whether Israel was investigating the alleged crimes itself; his office concludes it was not.

ICC issues arrest warrants for Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant
Read More »

25 March 2024 Khan informs the US administration of his decision and that warrants would be sought by the end of April.

15 April 2024 In London, Khan tells UK Justice Secretary Alex Chalk he will apply for the warrants; he had wanted to brief Foreign Secretary David Cameron directly, but Cameron was abroad.

19 April 2024 A senior US official warns Khan by phone of "disastrous consequences" if he proceeds; Khan says he rejected this, citing Israel's lack of cooperation.

23 April 2024 While Khan is on an official visit to Venezuela, Cameron phones him and says issuing warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant would be "like dropping a hydrogen bomb". Cameron spoke aggressively, told Khan he would "lose the dressing room" and be seen as "losing the plot", and said the UK would "defund the court and withdraw from the Rome Statute" if warrants were issued. Khan replied that this would mean "the rules-based system would be dead".

In an account of the episode in MEE journalist Peter Oborne's book, Complicit: Britain’s Role in the Destruction of Gaza, a source close to Cameron said that the call with Khan did take place and was “robust”. But the source said that rather than making a threat, Cameron pointed out that strong voices in the Conservative Party would push for defunding the ICC and withdrawing from the Rome Statute.

24 April 2024 12 Republican US senators (including Marco Rubio) send Khan a letter warning "Target Israel and we will target you." 

25 April 2024 British journalist Douglas Murray writes in the New York Post that Khan will seek warrants within days, before this is public knowledge.

26 April 2024 Netanyahu publicly criticises the ICC on social media, saying: “Under my leadership, Israel will never accept any attempt by the ICC to undermine its inherent right of self-defence.”

28 April 2024 Israel says it will allow Khan to visit Israel and Gaza, an unprecedented offer that delays the warrant applications.

29 April 2024 A colleague of Khan's raises harassment allegations against him in a private conversation.

30 April–1 May 2024 Khan describes meetings with western states and US officials that he characterises as efforts to dissuade him from proceeding.

Warrants filed, allegations surface (May 2024)

2 May 2024 The sexual misconduct/harassment allegations are first put to Khan in person by members of his team, on the same day, per his later ICC submission, that he had been planning to announce the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants. Khan separately meets Dutch counterterrorism officials over a security briefing about suspected Mossad activity in The Hague.

Exclusive: How Karim Khan’s Israel war crimes probe was derailed by threats, leaks and sex claims
Read More »

3 May 2024 A colleague of Khan refers the harassment allegations to the ICC's Internal Oversight Mechanism (IOM).

7 May 2024 The IOM's first inquiry closes after the complainant declines to cooperate.

19–20 May 2024 With Israel's promised permission letter for the Gaza visit still not delivered, Khan cancels the trip and, on 20 May, announces he is seeking arrest warrants for Netanyahu, Gallant, and Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar, Ismail Haniyeh and Mohammed Deif. In his public statement he says: "I insist that all attempts to impede, intimidate or improperly influence the officials of this Court must cease immediately."

21 May 2024 David Cameron publicly calls the warrant decision "a mistake", accusing the ICC of drawing a "moral equivalence" between Israeli and Hamas leaders.

10 June 2024 The outgoing Conservative government files a formal objection disputing ICC jurisdiction over Israeli nationals; the incoming Labour government drops the objection the following month, after the July 2024 general election.

Leaks, a second complaint, arrest warrants (October–November 2024)

17 October 2024 An anonymous Twitter account begins circulating details of the harassment allegations against Khan.

19 October 2024 The Mail on Sunday reports that ASP President Paivi Kaukoranta has confirmed the allegations exist; an official ASP statement follows later on 24 October.

October–November 2024 A second IOM investigation opens and closes after the complainant again declines to cooperate. 

11 November 2024 The ASP president subsequently decides to seek an outsourced UN investigation into Khan via the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS).

21 November 2024 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously approves and issues the arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant, the first time the court has targeted officials of a western-allied state. It also rejected two Israeli challenges to the case under Articles 19 and 18 of the Rome Statute.

Sanctions and threats (February–August 2025)

6 February 2025 Trump issues Executive Order 14203 imposing sanctions on ICC officials, with Khan as the initial target, over the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants; his US visa is revoked, his wife and children are barred from the US, and UK bank accounts are frozen.

19 May 2025 Khan takes voluntary leave pending the OIOS investigation; deputy prosecutors Nazhat Shameem Khan and Mame Mandiaye Niang take over the leadership of his office. 

May 2025 Shortly before going on leave, Khan had been preparing new warrant applications for Israeli ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir over West Bank settlement expansion.

‘Financial death penalty’: How US sanctions are upending the lives of ICC judges
Read More »

5 June 2025 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announces sanctions against four ICC judges: Beti Hohler (Slovenia) and Reine Alapini-Gansou (Benin) for their role in the Netanyahu/Gallant arrest warrants; and Luz del Carmen Ibanez Carranza (Peru) and Solomy Balungi Bossa (Uganda) for authorising the Afghanistan investigation. 

9 July 2026 The US sanctions UN Special Rapporteur on Palestine Francesca Albanese over her cooperation with the ICC. 

16 July 2025 ICC judges reject an Israeli request to withdraw the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants pending Israel's jurisdictional appeal.

20 August 2025 US imposes sanctions on judges Kimberly Prost (Canada) and Nicolas Yann Guillou (France), plus deputy prosecutors Nazhat Shameem Khan (Fiji) and Mame Mandiaye Niang (Senegal).

4 September 2025 US sanctions three Palestinian NGOs for cooperating with the ICC. 

13 October 2025 MEE reveals that Margareta Kassangana, a Polish diplomat and ASP vice president, met privately with Khan's accuser to discuss the case before the Bureau of the Assembly of States Parties, the court's govening body, referred the matter to the UN's OIOS in late 2024.

MEE also reports on a recorded summer 2025 phone call in which another bureau member, Uganda's ambassador Mirjam Blaak, is heard telling a colleague she believed Khan "may not come back", describing the complainant in personal terms, and repeating Netanyahu's since-debunked claim that Khan rushed the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants to pre-empt a "honey trap" defence. 

Disqualification bid and secret Smotrich filing (November 2025–May 2026)

17 November 2025 Israel formally asks the ICC to disqualify Khan from the Palestine investigation and withdraw the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants, citing the misconduct allegations as evidence of bias. The court has yet to rule on the request.

3 December 2025 The ASP's annual assembly in The Hague issues a declaration resisting US demands to drop the Palestine/Afghanistan investigations and amend the Rome Statute, without naming the US directly.

Exclusive: ICC prosecutor's office seeks arrest warrant for Israel's Smotrich
Read More »

10 December 2025 Khan submits a statement to the ICC's appeal chamber responding to Israel's disqualification request, describing for the first time a "senior UK government official" (confirmed by MEE as Cameron) who threatened UK funding withdrawal.

11 December 2025 The OIOS delivers its finalised report (150 pages, with roughly 5,000 pages of supporting evidence) to the ASP-appointed judicial panel for a legal determination.

18 December 2025 The US sanctions judges Gocha Lordkipanidze (Georgia) and Erdenebalsuren Damdin (Mongolia) after their rejection of Israel's appeal against the Gaza investigation.

22 January 2026 Responding to a Freedom of Information request, the UK Foreign Office confirms for the first time that the Cameron–Khan call took place on 23 April 2024.

9 March 2026 MEE breaks the story that a three-judge panel (Leona Theron of South Africa, Paul Lemmens of Belgium and Seymour Panton of Jamaica) unanimously concludes the OIOS findings "do not establish misconduct or breach of duty" by Khan. Lemmens, in a separate opinion, says he has "serious doubts" the allegations could ever meet the required standard, but joins the unanimous conclusion. 

23 March 2026 MEE reports that some bureau member states seek to sabotage the judges' panel's report. 

2 April 2026 A majority of the bureau votes to disregard the panel's conclusion and make its own assessment of the evidence. MEE names the 15 states that voted this way as Belgium, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Cyprus, Ecuador, Finland, Italy, Japan, Latvia, New Zealand, Poland, Slovenia, South Korea and Switzerland.

2 April 2026 The prosecutor's office secretly files an arrest warrant application for Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, alleging war crimes, crimes against humanity, and apartheid over West Bank settlement policy. It was the same warrant prepared by Khan before he went on leave but, as MEE reported, it was shelved for about a year.

Khan speaks out publicly for first time (April–May 2026)

29 April 2026 Khan gives his first public comments since going on leave, in an interview with journalist Mehdi Hasan on the outlet Zeteo. He says he thought the judges' panel finding "was the end of the matter" and is "perplexed" the bureau didn't close the case immediately. He calls the theory that he rushed the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants to distract from the allegations "baloney", noting that he told the US and others he would seek warrants in March 2024, before any allegation was raised. He says Russian and Israeli intelligence had been conducting "close surveillance" of him. 

8 May 2026 In an interview with MEE’s David Hearst Podcast, Khan accuses bureau members of running a "dangerous", biased campaign against him and says the disciplinary process is a "Khan-made process... specific to me".

Bureau's decision, run-up to vote (June–July 2026)

8 June 2026 The bureau votes to suspend Khan and, by a two-thirds majority, finds he committed "serious misconduct". MEE reports the vote as 14 in favour (Belgium, Brazil, Chile, Cyprus, Ecuador, Finland, Italy, Japan, Latvia, New Zealand, Poland, Slovenia, South Korea, Switzerland), four against (Kenya, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Uganda), three abstaining (Bolivia, Bosnia, South Africa).

The confidential decision, seen by MEE, frames the finding as Khan having "engaged in a sexual relationship" with the complainant that was improper given the power imbalance, a notable shift from the original non-consensual-conduct allegation. Khan denies any sexual relationship; the complainant's account centres on non-consensual conduct. Khan's lawyers say this reframed allegation was never put to him.

18 June 2026 MEE reveals the bureau has set 24 July, at UN headquarters in New York, as the date and venue for the full ASP's special session.

13 July 2026 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio explicitly threatens that Washington would "dismantle the ICC – brick by brick, if necessary".

16 July 2026 CNN airs an interview with Khan’s accuser going public for the first time, standing by her allegations of non-consensual sex. 

17 July 2026 ASP President Kaukoranta writes to member states confirming the bureau failed to reach the required majority on two separate retaliation allegations against Khan (from other staff members), which are now closed as unproven, distinct from the sexual misconduct finding still going to the full Assembly.

18 July 2026 Josep Borrell, the former EU foreign policy chief, writes that the bureau's process amounts to a "political vote" serving what he calls a US-Israeli "offensive" to "defang" the court, citing Rubio's stated intent to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick".

21 July 2026 Khan's legal team issues an open letter to ASP members stating that formal channels for Khan to make representations have been closed, that the ASP president discouraged states from meeting with his team, and that Khan and his lawyers have been denied accreditation to attend the 24 July session.

24 July 2026 (scheduled) The full ASP votes by secret ballot at UN headquarters, New York, under Article 46 of the Rome Statute, on the single combined motion covering both the misconduct finding and Khan's removal.

item.title: Govt working to normalise gas supply after FSRU technical fault
item.description:
The government is working to restore normal gas supply across the country after a technical fault at a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) disrupted the national gas distribution system.

The malfunction has reduced gas supply to the national grid by around 450 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd), the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources said in a statement today, Thursday.

Gas supply from the affected FSRU has been temporarily suspended due to the technical glitch, resulting in low gas pressure for industrial units, power plants, CNG filling stations and other consumers in different parts of the country.

The ministry said relevant agencies and technical experts are working round the clock to resolve the problem as quickly as possible.

Meanwhile, efforts are being made to ensure uninterrupted gas supply to emergency and priority sectors through optimal management of the available supply.

The statement noted that inadequate emphasis on domestic gas exploration and production in previous years increased the country's dependence on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG), making the national gas supply system vulnerable to disruptions whenever import infrastructure encounters operational problems.

To reduce that dependence, the government has undertaken short-, medium- and long-term initiatives to boost domestic gas production. As part of the plan, 100 gas wells will be drilled in phases across the country.

It also mentioned that the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) today, Thursday approved a Tk 7.29 billion project for drilling three gas wells in Begumganj and Sunamganj.

According to the statement, efforts are also underway to accelerate gas exploration in both onshore and offshore areas by inviting bids under the Production Sharing Contract (PSC) framework and encouraging investment from local and foreign companies.

The ministry added that gas exploration, well drilling, infrastructure development and the start of commercial production require considerable time, adding that the government is treating the issue as a top priority.

As part of its broader energy security strategy, the government has also initiated measures including inviting tenders for a fourth FSRU, assessing the feasibility of importing LNG from Malaysia through ISO tanks, reviewing pipeline and other transportation options to bring Bhola gas to the mainland, drilling new wells and carrying out workovers at existing gas fields, and diversifying energy import sources and supply infrastructure.

item.description:
The government has retired 17 senior police officers from public service, including three officers holding the rank of Deputy Inspector General (DIG).

The decision was announced in a gazette notification issued today, Thursday, by the Police-1 Branch of the Public Security Division under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The notification, signed by Senior Secretary Monzur Morshed Chowdhury, states that the officers have been retired in the public interest under Section 45 of the Government Service Act, 2018.

Those retired include three DIGs, 12 additional DIGs and two officers holding the rank of Superintendent of Police (SP).

According to the notification, the retired officers include Highway Police DIG Mohammad Abdullahil Baki, Bangladesh Police Academy (Sardah) DIG Md Walid Hossain, and CID DIG Sana Shaminur Rahman.

item.title: Experts for inclusive instant payment system to boost remittances, financial inclusion
item.description:
Financial sector leaders, central bank officials, and researchers gathered in Dhaka today to discuss how an Inclusive Instant Payment System (IIPS) could transform Bangladesh’s financial ecosystem by lowering transaction costs, reducing reliance on informal remittance channels, and driving digital inclusion.
The inception workshop, titled “Analysis of the Inclusive Instant Payment System (IIPS) in Bangladesh and Cross-Border Remittance as a Use Case,” was organized by the Policy Research Institute of Bangladesh (PRI) with support from the Gates Foundation.
Opening the session, PRI chairman Zaidi Sattar emphasized the critical macroeconomic role of remittances, which currently account for roughly 6% of Bangladesh’s GDP.
He called for strategic policies to shift these financial flows from basic consumption toward productive investment.
Sattar also highlighted the ongoing digital divide, pointing out that many migrant workers—such as the roughly 700,000 Bangladeshis living in Oman—still prefer informal hundi channels over formal banking due to existing barriers.
Addressing the technical groundwork, Mohammad Jahid Iqbal, additional director of the Payment System Department at Bangladesh Bank, revealed that the central bank is developing the IIPS using the open-source Mojaloop platform.
Launched in November 2025, the system aims to lower costs and connect banks, payment service providers, and eventually microfinance institutions.
It will also feature-phone access, simplified account opening, reduced transaction failures, and enhanced fraud protection using the Tazama toolkit.
Presenting research on the topic, PRI research director Bazlul Haque Khondker explained that an IIPS would make the payment ecosystem truly interoperable across banks and mobile financial services (MFS). Real-time, low-cost payment corridors could significantly curb reliance on informal channels and generate major savings for households.
PRI director MA Razzaque added that formalizing remittances will strengthen household resilience and national foreign-exchange reserves. To better understand migrant behaviors regarding speed, exchange rates, and trust, PRI is conducting a survey of Bangladeshi migrants across six key destination countries to inform practical policy solutions.
Single strategy for a cashless future
Ezazul Islam, director general of BIBM, noted that the long-term success of the IIPS will require a robust governance framework, fair commercial incentives, effective dispute resolution, and sound settlement risk management.
Sayed Shaikh Ibna Jilany, vice president of remittance at bKash Limited, added that private-sector integration must prioritize consumer protection, affordability, and user trust.
Ahsan H Mansur, distinguished fellow at PRI, argued that financial inclusion, IIPS deployment, and the transition toward a cashless economy must be treated as a single, unified national strategy.
He revealed that Bangladesh Bank currently spends approximately Tk20,000 crore annually on cash management—a cost that continues to rise.
To accelerate the shift to digital, he suggested that temporary incentives or subsidies for digital payments could offer greater long-term economic returns than subsidies in other sectors.
He also called for measures to make smartphones and internet services more affordable, restore public confidence in the banking sector, and create dedicated investment mechanisms to help repatriate an estimated $2 billion to $3 billion from the Bangladeshi diaspora.

item.title: Iraq’s impossible predicament: why the country is trapped between Iran and the US
item.description:
With the outbreak of this year’s war, Iraq’s balancing act between the two antagonists has collapsed, exposing a perilously fragile state

One week after the United States and Israel killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and ignited a regional war, drones started flying over Basra in southern Iraq. They were targeting Iraq’s oil industry. They hit an oilfield operated by BP, as well as a cargo terminal at Basra airport and a large compound that houses foreign companies that service the oil sector. Another attack on 6 March hit the same compound, striking offices and warehouses used by Halliburton and KBR, two US companies that have been in Iraq since the 2003 invasion. The attack sparked a massive fire that lit up the night sky.

In the wider war, it was not a particularly notable day – but in Iraq the strikes laid bare just how weak the state had become and “how easily sovereignty could be violated”, as one senior Iraqi security official put it to me. For 40 years, the US, Iran and Israel existed in an uneasy equilibrium of neither peace nor war. As this has come to a sudden, dramatic end, Iraq finds itself caught in the middle.

The spacecraft release black soot, rare metals, aluminum oxides and other pollutants with unknown effects.

item.title: The Guardian view on Britain’s uninhabitable homes: as temperatures rise, a new approach is needed | Editorial
item.description:
Sadiq Khan’s heat-ready plan for London is a sensible strategy for adaptation that should provide a roadmap for other cities

“Our ability to trust that our homes will keep us safe from the outside is under threat,” the geographer Sam Johnson-Schlee writes in Hot House, his recent book on how heat has transformed domestic life. This summer, high temperatures have become inescapable. People have coped with makeshift solutions: keeping curtains drawn, placing foil over windows or – for those who can afford one – plugging in an air-conditioning unit. Planning experts warn that, with only about half of councils requiring new buildings to include cooling strategies, many homes will become “death traps” as temperatures rise.

Britain’s homes weren’t built to cope with this. The country’s historically mild climate allowed developers to build houses without insulation, while industrialisation supplied plentiful coal to burn when temperatures dropped. Many homes are consequently drafty in winter and sweltering in summer. Unlike those in Mediterranean climates, British homes lack shutters and shaded communal spaces. While Ildefons Cerdà, Barcelona’s masterplanner, was designing housing blocks with cool courtyards and chamfered edges to allow breezes to flow, Britain’s Victorian builders were throwing up rows of terrace houses – many without cross-ventilation – and giving little thought to the movement of the sun.

item.title: The Guardian view on Europe’s demographic crisis: the young must not be left to deal with the consequences | Editorial
item.description:
A new Brussels study highlights the pace at which EU countries are ageing. A more informed public debate is overdue

Europe is ageing at pace as birthrates fall and people live longer. A new report by the European Commission, published this month, notes that 2012 marked the first year in which fewer people were born in EU countries than people died in them. By the middle of this century, nearly one in three EU residents will be 65 or older. The numbers of those over 80 will almost triple from 6% to 15%. The old continent is getting visibly greyer.

The transition to a “longevity society”, as the report’s authors describe it, is something to be celebrated. Many people are enjoying healthier, richer lives for longer, and redefining the meaning and possibilities of old age. But the statistics and direction of travel also point to immense social challenges, with implications for the way we work, intergenerational fairness and the future funding of care. Sadly, amid fraught and at times toxic debates about immigration and the cost of welfare, Europe’s politics is struggling to meet the moment.

item.title: Indian government seeks time on youth protesters' minister resignation demand
item.description:
Leaders of India’s youth-led “cockroach” movement said on Friday that the government ​has sought time until Saturday afternoon to respond to their demand for the education minister’s resignation over exam paper leaks, following talks between the two ‌sides.

The talks came hours after activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike, raising hopes that the two sides could reach a breakthrough after tens of thousands of angry youth converged in the capital Delhi this week to demand the minister’s resignation.

The anti-government protests represent the biggest youth challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi since he came to power in 2014. Opposition parties have echoed the movement’s demands and have disrupted ​the monsoon session of parliament that began this week.

Friday’s talks were held between senior federal ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh on one side, and Saurav Das ​and Ashutosh Ranka, spokespersons of the self-named Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth movement, on the other.

The CJP leaders said they had conveyed that ⁠nothing would be acceptable to them without Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation, and warned that without this, protests would spread.

“The government has asked for time until tomorrow afternoon to respond ​on this point (the resignation),” Ranka told reporters. “We hope the government will dismiss Dharmendra Pradhan at the earliest, or that he will resign, so that we can bring this matter to ​a conclusion.”

Minister Nadda said the talks were cordial.

“They had three main demands. We have told them we will meet you tomorrow afternoon and discuss the demands,” he said.

Scattered protests across the country

Besides the resignation of Pradhan, CJP wants police cases filed against protesters dropped, and compensation paid to families of more than a dozen students who local media reported took their own lives after the exam paper leak in ​May.

Although the protesters agreed to hold talks, they had also called for nationwide demonstrations on Friday over alleged police brutality against protesters who marched on parliament on Monday.

While thousands ​of protesters continued to gather at the main protest site of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, there were reports of scattered protests across the country.

Students, youth activists and opposition supporters staged protests in ‌the states ⁠of West Bengal, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, holding placards demanding Pradhan’s resignation and boycotting classes in some places, local media reported.

Parliament was disrupted and suspended again on Friday as opposition lawmakers also demanded Pradhan’s resignation, with no business conducted for the entire week.

The protests by CJP began as an online satire and involved only a few hundred young people when they were first launched. But they grew to pull in millions of online followers when a national medical school entrance test was cancelled in May because the question paper was leaked ​earlier, affecting about 2 million students.

Tens of thousands ​of supporters of the movement marched on ⁠parliament in violation of a ban on Monday and clashed with police when they were pushed back with tear gas and beaten with batons.

Metro stations shut, mobile internet blocked again

The movement’s surge in popularity reflects frustrations among young Indians over issues such as job shortages, as ​well as frequent exam leaks, analysts say.

The Delhi Metro Rail Corp. shut down 17 stations in and around central Delhi on Friday, ​the third time this week ⁠it resorted to such a large-scale closure of the system, which is the lifeline of the capital.

The government extended a mobile internet shutdown in the area until midnight on Friday, two industry sources told Reuters.

The government also defended surveillance by police at the protest site, saying in court that there was no right to privacy in a public space when there is a ⁠legitimate state interest.

Youth-led, ​street protests in neighbouring Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal have brought down governments in recent years.

Although national elections ​are due only by April 2029, key states like the most populous, Uttar Pradesh, run by Modi’s party, his home state of Gujarat, and Punjab, vote next year and anti-government sentiment could have an impact, analysts say.

item.title: Bangladesh President Shahabuddin, 76, resigns citing health concerns
item.description:
Bangladesh President Mohammed Shahabuddin, a former ally of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina, has resigned citing serious health issues, his office said on Friday.

Shahabuddin, 76, has held the largely ceremonial post of president since April 2023, a period that included volatile months after Hasina’s flight to India following a student-led uprising against her rule in 2024.

“Recent medical examinations have diagnosed me with a condition known as autonomic neuropathy. Due to this condition, I occasionally experience momentary loss of consciousness,” Shahabuddin said in a statement released by his press secretary.

The speaker of the Jatiya Sangsad, the national parliament, will perform the duties of the president until a new one is elected, the statement said.

Shahabuddin also cited his deteriorating health in a resignation letter to the speaker of parliament, seen by AFP.

“Due to worsening physical and mental incapacity… it is no longer possible for me to properly discharge the responsibilities of an important constitutional office such as the presidency,” it said.

Shahabuddin, widely known as “Chuppu”, was elected by parliament in 2023 with support from Hasina’s Awami League.

When a student revolt ousted the autocratic Hasina in 2024, calls mounted for the president to be removed, too.

Shahabuddin was accused of speaking to Hasina by phone while he was undergoing medical treatment in London in May, an allegation he has denied.

Shahabuddin’s resignation would leave Hasina with no allies in high office five months before her planned return.

Her Awami League party is banned, and many of its leaders and activists have been jailed or gone into hiding since the deadly student-led uprising in 2024.

item.title: India, Pakistan among teams handed direct Asian Games men's cricket knockout berths
item.description:
India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka secured direct entry into the men’s cricket knockout stage at the 2026 Asian Games after the draw was announced on Thursday.

The 10-team men’s competition, starting from September 24 in Nagoya, will begin with a preliminary round featuring Afghanistan, Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, Nepal and Oman competing for the remaining quarter-final berths.

Afghanistan, Japan and Nepal were drawn in Group A, while Hong Kong, Malaysia and Oman were placed in Group B. The top two teams from each group will advance to the knockout stage to join the four seeded sides.

The women’s tournament, scheduled from September 17-22, features eight teams and will begin at the quarter-final stage. Defending champions India will face hosts Japan, Bangladesh will take on China, Sri Lanka will meet Malaysia, and Pakistan will play Thailand.

All matches in both competitions will be played in the Twenty20 format.

India swept the cricket gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games, held in 2023 in Hangzhou, claiming both the men’s and women’s titles.

item.title: Brian Lara Stadium hosts maiden Test as West Indies face Pakistan
item.description:
West Indies and Pakistan meet at Test cricket’s newest venue in Trinidad on Saturday at the start of a two-match series in which the home side will be enjoying rare favoured status against the visitors.

Brian Lara Stadium, located in the south of the island, has previously hosted one-day and T20 internationals along with regional first-class fixtures.

It becomes the nation’s second Test match venue and 13th in the West Indies, drawing it alongside Queen’s Park Oval in the capital, Port of Spain, the venue of the second Test a week later.

Roston Chase enjoyed his first match and series wins as West Indies Test captain just three weeks ago when the Caribbean team demolished Sri Lanka by an innings and 217 runs and then played out a draw in the second and final Test, both matches played in Antigua.

Chase missed the recent ODI series loss to New Zealand with an injury to his right index finger.

“Roston is a fighter. I know he’s not going to want to miss any Test cricket,” West Indies head coach Daren Sammy said.

“I’m pretty sure Dr. Byam (team physio Denis Byam) has a way of keeping guys on the park, so I’m pretty sure Roston will be ready for the first Test.”

It was their first home Test series triumph since a 2-0 sweep of Bangladesh in 2022, a result which also gave them their last consecutive series wins anywhere as the whitewash of the Bangladeshis was preceded by a notable 1-0 home triumph over England in a three-Test contest.

West Indies are not expected to make significant alterations to the winning combination from the Sri Lankan series, although left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican is likely to come into consideration at the expense of fast-medium bowler Anderson Phillip given the expectation of a pitch favouring spin later in the match.

In-form Ali

In stark contrast, Pakistan have once again revamped their squad in the aftermath of a 2-0 series loss in Bangladesh two months ago with batsman Babar Azam returning as captain in place of Shan Masood in hope of reviving their Test fortunes.

Babar and opening batsman Azan Awais both compiled hundreds in the lone warm-up match against a West Indies Select XI at the weekend while most of the other main batsmen also got confidence-boosting runs.

However the most encouraging aspect of the match in batting-friendly conditions for the tourists was the bowling of pacer Mohammad Ali, who took five wickets in the first innings and will be relied upon, together with the other members of the restructured pace armoury, to give Pakistan a chance to end a miserable run of seven consecutive Test match losses away from home.

Their last visit to the Caribbean in 2021 finished in a 1-1 draw after two Tests in Kingston while the teams’ most recent Test encounters were in the spin-dominant Multan in January of 2025 when the West Indies trumped Pakistan at their own game in the second match to also leave that series at 1-1.

This meeting of two unpredictable sides carries the additional dimension of intervention by the elements as the July/August period is usually one of significant rainfall in the southern Caribbean.

While Trinidad has enjoyed hot, sunny conditions in the days leading up to the first Test, there is certainly no guarantee that such pleasant cricketing weather will be sustained over the fortnight of this short series.

item.title: Iran military says attacked US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait
item.description:
Iran’s military said on Friday it carried out drone strikes against several American military facilities and bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait in retaliation for the latest US attacks against the Islamic Republic.
“This morning, the fuel tanks, large equipment warehouses and silos, and the barracks of the US terrorist army forces at the Isa Air Base in Bahrain were targeted by Arash kamikaze drones,” the army said in a statement carried by state TV.
An AFP journalist in Bahrain reported an explosion and the sounding of warning sirens Friday, though it was not immediately clear if the two events were linked.
There was no confirmation from the US of any targeting of its facilities or personnel.
The Iranian army also claimed drone attacks against Jordan, targeting “aircraft hangars, aviation maintenance hangars and a barracks” at Al-Azraq base.
Jordan has not reported any strikes in the last few hours.
In a separate statement, the Iranian army said it had launched drones at US equipment warehouses in Camp Udairi and the site of American military personnel in Camp Doha and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
Meanwhile, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, claiming to have destroyed an ammunition depot and inflicted casualties among US personnel.
They also claimed attacks on equipment storage silos at Camp Udairi in Kuwait and a US Fifth Fleet watchtower in Bahrain.
Tehran argues that any facility or base in the Middle East that the US military uses for strikes on Iran is considered a legitimate target for retaliation.

item.title: UN urges evacuation of 6,000 sailors stranded in Hormuz strait
item.description:
The United Nations on Friday urged countries involved in the Middle East war to help evacuate and repatriate some 6,000 sailors stranded in the Strait of Hormuz.
UN human rights chief Volker Turk called for urgent action to remedy the plight of thousands of stranded seafarers, who are facing “a dire humanitarian and human rights crisis” in the waterway, his spokeswoman Shabia Mantoo said.
The International Maritime Organization has said there are at least 6,000 seafarers on hundreds of vessels who are stranded in the strait, unable to evacuate during the ceasefire.
“Parties to the conflict should urgently work to facilitate safe passage for stranded seafarers to safely evacuate and disembark, as well as ensure the delivery of critical supplies,” Mantoo told a press conference in Geneva.
“Attacks against civilian vessels are unacceptable and must stop. They are protected under international humanitarian law.”
Turk is urging states, ship owners and all other relevant actors to “urgently ensure the protection of stranded seafarers”, including through consular assistance and providing essential supplies, “and by facilitating evacuations and repatriations,” Mantoo added.
The United States launched fresh strikes on Iran on Friday after Tehran-backed Houthi rebels attacked oil tankers in the Red Sea, marking an escalation that pushed crude prices past $100 a barrel.
The US military insisted that the Strait of Hormuz -- through which one fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war -- was “open for transit” after Iran pressed on with attacks on tankers using the route in a bid to strongarm them into paying for safe passage.

Volker Turk's term as UN human rights chief extended despite US warnings
item.description:
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to renew Volker Turk’s mandate as high commissioner for human rights for four years despite strong opposition from the United States, Russia and Israel.

By a vote of 144 in favour, 10 against, and 13 abstentions, the assembly approved the renewal, beginning October 12, 2026, as proposed by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

An alternative proposal from Russia to extend the mandate by only a few months, until December 31, 2026, was overwhelmingly rejected, as was the US request to postpone the vote.

Ambassador Jeff Bartos, US representative for UN management and reform, criticised the four-year renewal on both procedural and substantive grounds, accusing Guterres of having rushed the process.

“Make no mistake: If this assembly tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts, there will be consequences.

“The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding,” he warned just before the vote, accusing Guterres of having rushed the timetable “to hand his long-term friend a four-year executive payout”.

French Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, however, described Turk as “a voice of conscience” who had demonstrated “rigour and impartiality” during his first term.

Turk, an Austrian jurist, has served as high commissioner since October 2022. He has emphasised the universality of human rights and the need to apply international law equally.

During his tenure, he has been outspoken on the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the war in Gaza, Afghanistan, Sudan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Nicaragua.

But he’s also been criticised for not taking more decisive positions on Cuba, the plight of Uyghurs in Xinjiang, China, and for not directly using the word “genocide” in reference to Gaza, unlike several UN experts and rapporteurs.

Turk’s stances have earned him sharp criticism from several governments, notably Russia and Israel.

Both nations’ ambassadors voiced opposition Friday to his renewal, saying Guterres, whose term as secretary-general expires at the end of the year, should have left the selection of the human rights commissioner to his successor.

Maldives: FM Khalilur’s visit sets stage for enhanced cooperation in years ahead
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman arrived in the Maldives on Saturday to pay an official visit, which is seen as a "significant milestone" in further strengthening the longstanding and cordial relations between Bangladesh and the Maldives.
“The visit sets the stage for enhanced cooperation in the years ahead,” said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Maldives.
Dr Khalilur was received by the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives, Iruthisham Adam, and senior officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The foreign minister is visiting the Maldives from July 25-27 as a "special guest" of the government of Maldives to attend the celebrations marking the 61st anniversary of the Independence of the Republic of Maldives.
Dr Khalilur arrived in the Maldives via Doha from Manila, Philippines, a senior official told UNB.
During the visit, Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur is scheduled to pay a courtesy call on the President of the Republic of Maldives Dr Mohamed Muizzu and meet with Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam.
The discussions will focus on further strengthening the longstanding partnership between the Maldives and Bangladesh, reviewing the broad spectrum of bilateral cooperation, and exploring new opportunities to expand collaboration in areas of mutual interest.
The two ministers will also exchange views on regional and international developments and reaffirm their commitment to continued cooperation in regional and multilateral fora.
This is the first official visit to the Maldives by Dr Khalilur since assuming office as the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh on February 17, 2026.

item.title: Law minister: All must be treated with equal dignity, not divided by religion
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Saturday said there is no need to identify or divide people on the basis of religion, stressing that every citizen of Bangladesh must be treated with equal dignity and equal rights.
"Just as a person's blood does not change color because of their religion, citizens' rights cannot vary on religious grounds either. If we can value and respect everyone as human beings, only then will it be possible to eliminate communal divisions and discrimination," he said.
The law minister said this while speaking as the chief guest at the biennial conference of the Mohanogor Sarbojanin Puja Committee held at the premises of the Dhakeshwari National Temple in the capital on Saturday noon.
He said Bangladesh should be built as a country where every citizen naturally feels safe and can celebrate religious festivals without fear or disruption.
"The minister said everyone must refrain from using religion for politics or electoral gains. Instead, politics should be guided by a commitment to public welfare, development, good governance and human values. The present government's goal is to create an environment in which every citizen can practice his or her religion freely and without hindrance," he added.
Referring to the encroachment on the land of the Dhakeshwari National Temple, the law minister said the government would take the necessary steps to recover the occupied property.
He said no land grabber, criminal or mafia syndicate would be allowed to retain possession of the temple's property permanently and assured the authorities of the government's full cooperation in this regard.
Prime Minister's Special Assistant on Hindu, Buddhist, Christian and Ethnic Minority Affairs Bijon Kanti Sarkar, Dhaka-7 lawmaker Hamidur Rahman, Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad President Basudeb Dhar, its General Secretary Santosh Sharma, Mohanogor Sarbojanin Puja Committee President Jayanta Kumar Dev, its General Secretary Dr Tapas Chandra Pal, and leaders of the Dhakeshwari National Temple Management Committee addressed the function, among others.

item.title: WHO: Around 9600 people die from drowning each year in Bangladesh
item.description:
World Health Organization (WHO) has called for accelerated action to prevent drowning in Bangladesh, warning that around 9,600 people die from drowning in the country each year despite the availability of proven, life-saving interventions.
For children aged 1-4 years, drowning is the leading cause of death, with thousands of children, particularly those living in rural and low-income communities, losing their lives each year in incidents that are largely preventable.
Most drowning deaths among children under 5 occur within 20 metres of the home, mainly in ponds, ditches and water containers.
Every year on July 25, the world marks World Drowning Prevention Day to raise awareness that drowning deaths are preventable and to promote proven actions that save lives.
On World Drowning Prevention Day, WHO has called for accelerated action in Bangladesh to build on the country's leadership in drowning prevention through greater investment in evidence-based interventions, stronger partnerships and sustained action to address one of the world's most preventable yet overlooked public health challenges.
Every year, drowning claims more than 300 000 lives worldwide - equivalent to nearly 30 deaths per hour.
Almost one-quarter of these deaths occur among children under the age of 5. Globally, drowning is among the 10 leading causes of death for children aged 5-14 years.
Together, the 10 countries of the WHO South-East Asia Region account for 28% of drowning deaths worldwide.
"Drowning is a silent but preventable public health crisis. Every drowning death represents a tragedy that can and must be prevented,” said Dr Ahmed Jamsheed Mohamed, WHO Representative to Bangladesh.
“As we observe World Drowning Prevention Day, WHO reaffirms its commitment to supporting evidence-based action, stronger partnerships and increased investment in proven interventions that reduce drowning deaths.”
Bangladesh has demonstrated strong leadership in advancing drowning prevention nationally and globally, WHO said.
It has championed international resolutions on drowning prevention at both the United Nations General Assembly and the World Health Assembly, while the government-endorsed National Drowning Prevention Strategy and Action Plan (2025–2030) provides a framework for scaling up evidence-based interventions, including Anchal centres (community childcare centres), SwimSafe programmes (survival swimming education) and first responder training.
However, to build on this progress, greater urgency and sustained investment are needed to unlock the full health, social and economic benefits of evidence-based interventions, WHO said.
Evidence from Bangladesh shows that proven interventions save lives while delivering strong economic returns, with every US$1 invested estimated to generate US$ 9 in social and economic benefits.
On World Drowning Prevention Day, WHO highlighted four priority areas for action.
First, integrating drowning prevention into national health, education and disaster risk reduction policies. This is essential to ensuring a coordinated and sustainable response, recognizing that drowning is not only a water safety issue but also a major public health challenge that intersects with child health, education, disaster preparedness and community development.
Second, scaling up proven interventions that reduce drowning deaths such as Anchal centres, SwimSafe programmes and first responder training. Expanding access to these interventions, particularly in rural and underserved communities, will save thousands of lives each year while helping children develop lifelong water safety skills.
Third, strengthening partnerships and sustaining community engagement. By working together and building on their respective strengths, local authorities, development partners, civil society organizations, academic institutions, the private sector and communities can increase the reach of effective interventions, promote safer behaviours and foster a culture of water safety that protects future generations.
Fourth, enhancing investment in research, surveillance and data systems. Strengthening the evidence base on drowning and drowning prevention will support better decision-making, guide future policy and programme development and enable Bangladesh to measure progress towards reducing drowning deaths and achieving related Sustainable Development Goal targets.
"We know how to prevent drowning. The challenge now is to take proven interventions to scale and ensure they reach every child and every community at risk. With sustained political commitment, strong partnerships and continued investment, we can dramatically reduce drowning deaths and save thousands of lives each year," said Dr Ahmed Jamsheed Mohamed.
On World Drowning Prevention Day, WHO called on governments, partners and communities to unite behind proven solutions that save lives. Together, we can protect children, strengthen communities and ensure that far fewer families experience the devastating and preventable loss of a loved one to drowning.

item.title: BBS survey: Over 57% of Bangladeshi households now have internet access
item.description:
More than half of Bangladeshi households now have internet access, reflecting the country's steady digital transformation, according to the latest quarterly Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS).
The survey found that 57.4% of households had internet access during the January-March 2026 quarter, up from 55.1% recorded in the annual estimate for FY2024-25. Internet use among people aged five and above also rose to 58.6%, while household smartphone ownership increased to 73.4%.
The findings suggest digital connectivity continues to expand across Bangladesh, driven by growing internet adoption and wider access to smartphones and computers.
According to the report, internet usage has maintained an upward trend throughout the current fiscal year.
Among people aged five and above, internet use rose from 48.9% in the first quarter (July-September 2025) to 58.4% in the second quarter (October-December 2025), before edging up to 58.6% in the third quarter.
Household internet access followed a similar trajectory, increasing from 55.1% in the previous fiscal year's annual estimate to 57.4% in the latest quarter.
The figures point to continued growth in digital services, supported by rising smartphone adoption and greater reliance on online platforms for communication, education, financial services and commerce.
Despite the overall expansion in digital connectivity, the survey recorded a marginal decline in personal mobile phone ownership. The share of individuals owning a mobile phone slipped to 65.4% in the third quarter from 65.5% in the previous quarter, although it remained well above the 56.5% recorded in the first quarter.
Overall mobile phone usage—including shared access to phones—continued to edge upward, reaching 89.5%, compared with 89.4% in the previous quarter.
The data indicate that while personal ownership has largely stabilised, access to mobile communication is now nearly universal through both personal and shared devices.
Computer use also continued its gradual rise. The proportion of individuals using computers increased to 11.7% in the January-March quarter, compared with 11.4% in the previous quarter and 10% in the first quarter of the fiscal year.
At the household level, mobile phone ownership is almost universal, with 98.9% of households owning at least one mobile phone. Smartphone ownership also climbed steadily, rising from 72.7% in FY2024-25 to 73.4% in the latest quarter.
Meanwhile, landline telephone use continued its long-term decline, with only 0.7% of households reporting a landline, down from 0.8% a year earlier. The survey found that 98.2% of households now rely exclusively on mobile phones as their primary means of communication.
Ownership of traditional media devices, including televisions and radios, remained largely unchanged during the quarter.
Electricity access, however, slipped slightly, with household electricity coverage falling from 98.9% in the first quarter to 98.5% in the third quarter.
The quarterly ICT survey collected information from 2,568 sample areas nationwide.
BBS interviewed 61,632 households each quarter, totaling 246,528 households annually, with data collected by 214 trained enumerators.
According to the statistical agency, this is its second district-representative large-scale ICT survey since 2013.
BBS said the quarterly findings will be consolidated into a comprehensive annual report. The data will contribute to 22 ICT indicators monitored by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and support Bangladesh's progress in tracking the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The latest findings suggest Bangladesh's digital ecosystem continues to strengthen, with rising internet access and smartphone adoption accelerating the country's transition to a more digitally connected economy.

item.title: Maritime ports asked to hoist cautionary signal No 3
item.description:
Maritime ports of Chittagong, Cox's Bazar, Mongla and Payra have been advised to hoist local cautionary signal No 3 as a low-pressure area has formed over Northwest Bay and adjoining Gangetic West Bengal-North Odisha coasts.
Under its influence, squally weather may affect the Maritime Ports, North Bay and adjoining Coastal areas of Bangladesh, said a special bulletin of the Met office.
All fishing boats and trawlers over North Bay have been advised to come close to the coast and proceed with caution till further notice.
